content: Postoperative pain is a significant challenge in pediatric care, as it can lead to both functional and organic complications that may negatively impact surgical outcomes. Cleft lip, one of the most common craniofacial birth defects, requires early surgical intervention. Following cleft lip repair, children often experience moderate to severe pain due to the sensitivity of the surgical site. Infraorbital nerve block, when used in conjunction with general anesthesia, has been proposed as a method to alleviate postoperative pain in these cases. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of infraorbital nerve block in managing postoperative pain in children undergoing cleft lip repair. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, up to June 17, 2015. Ongoing trials were also identified through platforms such as ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry. Randomized controlled trials comparing infraorbital nerve block to other analgesic methods, placebo, or no intervention were included. The review considered the type of drug, dosage, and route of administration used in each study. The perioperative period was defined as encompassing preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative phases. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data, with disagreements resolved by consulting a third reviewer. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE system. Eight studies involving 353 children were included in the review. These studies varied in terms of the drugs used (lignocaine or bupivacaine), observation periods, and methods of outcome measurement, which limited the ability to perform meta-analyses. When comparing infraorbital nerve block to placebo, the intervention group showed significantly lower mean postoperative pain scores (standardized mean difference [SMD] -3.54, 95% confidence interval [CI] -6.13 to -0.95; very low-quality evidence). One study reported a longer duration of analgesia in the intervention group (mean difference [MD] 8.26 hours, 95% CI 5.41 to 11.11; very low-quality evidence) and reduced need for supplemental analgesics (risk ratio [RR] 0.05, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.18; low-quality evidence). When comparing infraorbital nerve block to intravenous analgesia, the intervention group again demonstrated lower mean postoperative pain scores (SMD -1.50, 95% CI -2.40 to -0.60; very low-quality evidence) and a shorter time to feeding (MD -9.45 minutes, 95% CI -17.37 to -1.53; moderate-quality evidence). No significant adverse events were reported in association with the nerve block, although three studies did not address this outcome. Five of the eight studies reported no unwanted side effects. The overall risk of bias in the included studies was low or unclear. However, the quality of evidence was downgraded due to small sample sizes, lack of detailed information on randomization and allocation concealment, and variability in outcome reporting. In conclusion, there is lowto very low-quality evidence suggesting that infraorbital nerve block with lignocaine or bupivacaine may be more effective than placebo or intravenous analgesia in reducing postoperative pain in children undergoing cleft lip repair. Further research with larger sample sizes is needed. Future studies should aim to standardize observation periods, outcome measurement tools, and age group stratification to improve the reliability of findings.
